title: DATA 201 Week 3 Session 1
text:
Attributes

What is an attribute?

Qualities and characteristics that describe a data object or instance
Example: Company surveying their employee’s happiness
Data object:  Employee 
Attributes: job position, working-hours satisifaction, team satisfaction

title: DATA 201 Week 3 Session 1
text:
Levels of measurement

Nominal
Ordinal
Interval
Ratio

title: DATA 201 Week 3 Session 1
text:
Nominal

Labels that have no natural order; order is interchangeable
Gender: female, male
Eye colour: brown, green, blue
Place you live: city, suburbs, rural
Languages that you speak: English, French, Spanish
If there are only two categories, we can say that it is binary/dichotomous

yes/no

title: DATA 201 Week 3 Session 1
text:
Ordinal

labels that have a natural/or meaningful order
Very unsatisfied, unsatisfied, neutral, satisfied, very satisfied

satisfied is better than unsatisfied

School grades: A is better than B and B is better than C
Frequency of watching TV

1 = daily
2 = several times a week
3 = several times a month
4 = never

title: DATA 201 Week 3 Session 1
text:
Ratio

Ratio scale has equal intervals
Has a meaningful zero

0 grams means something has no mass

Comparisons are meaningful

100 cm is twice as long as 50 cm
5kgs is half as heavy as 10 kgs

title: DATA 201 Week 3 Session 1
text:
Interval

Also has equal intervals, but no meaningful zero
Difference between 10°C and 20°C is the same size as 20°C and 30°C

BUT 20°C is not twice as hot as 10°C
0°C is not an absolute/meaningful zero

Kelvins has an absolute zero, so it would be ratio

Data-Ink Ratio

Concept introduced by Edward Tufte
In a graphic, large portion of the ink should present data-information
Data ink = bars, lines, dots (actual data)
Non-data ink = borders, gridlines, backgrounds, decorative elements
Criticisms on minimalism: Paper

The idea here is that data should be used thoughtfully

Radio: advertising dollars spent on Radio
Newspaper: advertising dollars spent on Newspaper
Sales: sales of a single product in a given market (in thousands of units)

title: DATA 201 Week 9: Quantitative Analysis
text:
Histograms: Distribution

Histograms show the distribution on the diagonal

Distribution: frequency of values in a dataset
Normal/Symmetric? Many values near the centre
Uniform? The frequency of values are about the same, looks boxy
Right/Left skewed? Values are mostly low or high
Bimodal? (two peaks) There could be two unique distributions

title: DATA 201 Week 9: Quantitative Analysis
text:
Histograms: Skewness

Skewness

Positive Skew: mean > median
Negative Skew: mean < median
No skew: mean = median = mode

title: DATA 201 Week 9: Quantitative Analysis
text:
Correlation Coefficient

All the data points get represented as a single value
Pearson’s r measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship
Ranges from -1 to +1

+1: perfect positive (as X goes up, Y goes up)
0: no linear relationship
-1: perfect negative (as X goes up, Y goes down)

Rough guide: |r| < 0.3 weak, 0.3 to 0.7 moderate, > 0.7 strong
Let’s do it in Excel!


Explain correlation first: one number summarizing how tightly the points hug a line. Remind them correlation is not causation, and that r only captures linear patterns (a perfect U-shape can have r near 0). Negative means that as x feature goes up, then the y value decreases

title: DATA 201 Week 9: Quantitative Analysis
text:
Heatmap for Correlation

A heatmap turns the matrix into colour so patterns pop out
In Excel: select the matrix → Home → Conditional Formatting → Color Scales
Dark = strong, light = weak
Look for:

Strong correlations with the target (Sales)
Strong correlations between predictors (multicollinearity)

PowerBI


Show the heatmap after the numeric matrix so they can connect the colours to the values. Point out that Radio and Newspaper are correlated, which may matter later.

title: DATA 201 Week 9: Quantitative Analysis
text:
From Correlation to Regression

Correlation: how strongly are two variables related?
Regression: what is the relationship, and can we predict with it?
Simple linear regression:

\[\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\]

\(\beta_0\) is the intercept: predicted Sales when spend is 0
\(\beta_1\) is the slope: change in Sales for each additional unit of spend
The “best” line minimizes the sum of squared residuals (least squares)

title: DATA 201 Week 9: Quantitative Analysis
text:
Which Line Is “Best”?

Many lines could be drawn through the data
Each point misses the line by some amount: its residual
Square the misses and add them up to score a line
Squaring stops over- and under-predictions from cancelling out
The least squares line has the smallest total score

title: DATA 201 Week 9: Quantitative Analysis

title: DATA 201 Week 9: Quantitative Analysis
section: Residuals: What the Line Gets Wrong
text:
Residuals: What the Line Gets Wrong

Residual = actual value − predicted value

\[e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i\]

Positive residual: the line under-predicted
Negative residual: the line over-predicted
Least squares picks the line that makes this as small as possible:

title: DATA 201 Week 9: Quantitative Analysis
text:
Multiple R

Multiple R = 0.947212034
How strongly the predictors, taken together, relate to Sales
If only one predictor, it’s the same as the correlation coefficient
Closer to 1 means a stronger relationship

title: DATA 201 Week 9: Quantitative Analysis
text:
R Square (R²)

R Square = 0.897210638
Proportion of variance in response variable (Sales) using the predictor variables (TV, Radio, Newspaper)

Value of 1 => variability in response can be explained by predictors
Value of 0 => variability in response cannot be explained by predictors



Common mistake: R² of 0.61 does not mean the predictions are 61% accurate. It means 61% of the variation in Sales is accounted for. R² never goes down when you add variables, which is why adjusted R² exists. 0.6 is strong in marketing, but would be weak in physics.

title: DATA 201 Week 9: Quantitative Analysis
text:
Standard Error

Standard Error = 1.685510373
The typical size of a prediction miss, in the units of Sales
Smaller is better


Standard error is often more useful than R² for judging practical accuracy, because it’s in real units. Roughly 95% of actual values fall within two standard errors of the prediction.

title: DATA 201 Week 9: Quantitative Analysis
text:
Coefficients: The Effect

Intercept = 2.939

Predicted Sales when $0 is spent on all three media of advertising (about 2,900 units)

TV = 0.0458

For each extra $1,000 spent on TV ads, we predict that about 46 more units sold

Radio = 0.1885

Each each extra $1,000 spent on radio ads, we predict that about 189 more units sold

These values are if other variables are constant
This doesn’t mean that radio is better than TV


Spend is in thousands of dollars and Sales is in thousands of units, so 0.0458 means 45.8 units per $1,000. Radio returns roughly 4x as many units per dollar as TV. The intercept is an extrapolation if no market has $0 spend on all three media.

title: DATA 201 Week 9: Quantitative Analysis
text:
Coefficients: Newspaper

Newspaper = -0.0010

Essentially zero, and slightly negative

Each extra $1,000 on newspaper goes with about 1 fewer unit

Too small to matter

The sign shows direction and the size shows strength


Don’t read the negative sign as “newspaper ads hurt sales.” The estimate is statistically indistinguishable from zero, as the p-value and confidence interval will show.

title: DATA 201 Week 9: Quantitative Analysis
text:
Coefficients: Can We Trust It?

Standard Error: how much the estimate would wobble with different data

Small relative to the coefficient means a precise estimate

t Stat: the coefficient measured in standard errors

Rule of thumb: |t| > 2 is significant
TV: 32.8, Radio: 21.9, Newspaper: -0.18

title: DATA 201 Week 9: Quantitative Analysis
text:
P-Value

indicates how likely a statistical result occured by chance
small p value:

statistically significant, unlikely to be chance alone
accept alternative hypothesis
Alternative hypothesis: theory you are trying to prove

high p value:

statistically non-significant, likely to be chance
failed to reject null-hypothesis
Null hypothesis: theory you are trying to disprove

p-values range from: 0 - 0.1


Newspaper’s standard error (0.0059) is much larger than its coefficient (0.0010), so the t stat is near 0. A p-value of 0.86 means that if newspaper truly had no effect, we’d see an estimate this size about 86% of the time just by chance.

title: DATA 201 Week 9: Quantitative Analysis
text:
Coefficients: Confidence Interval

Lower / Upper 95%: the range of plausible values for the true effect
TV: 0.043 to 0.049

Each $1,000 adds between 43 and 49 units

Radio: 0.172 to 0.206

Each $1,000 adds between 172 and 206 units

Newspaper: -0.013 to 0.011

The range includes 0, so we can’t rule out no effect



Newspaper’s “no effect” means no added value given TV and Radio are already in the model. It doesn’t prove newspaper ads never work. Newspaper looked related to Sales in the correlation matrix (r = 0.23) only because it correlates with Radio (r = 0.35). The key is whether the interval includes zero: - TV: Its interval is entirely positive, supporting a positive coefficient. - Radio: Its interval is entirely positive, also supporting a positive coefficient. - Newspaper: Its interval includes zero, meaning the true coefficient could be negative, zero, or positive under the model.

title: DATA 201 Week 9: Quantitative Analysis
text:
Key Takeaways

Scatterplot matrices give a quick visual of trends, distributions, and outliers
Correlation (r) summarizes the strength and direction of a linear relationship
Heatmaps make a correlation matrix easy to scan
Regression quantifies the relationship and enables prediction
